summary: Added a Timeline playback screen (Workspace nav, beside Live Views) that plays recorded footage by the clock instead of by file: a scrub bar shaded from the same merged footage spans the coverage strip reports, seeking across segment boundaries automatically, up to 8 cameras synchronised against one moment, playback speed 0.25x-8x, and detection events plotted as clickable jump marks. Backed by two new endpoints, GET /api/recording/timeline (segment index + coverage over a window) and GET /api/recording/timeline/seek (resolve one wall-clock moment to a playable segment + offset per camera, snapping forward and reporting the gap when the moment isn't covered), both capped at 8 cameras and a 31-day window per request and refusing rather than truncating a camera with too many segments in range. The coverage-span merge was factored out of the existing coverage service so the bar, the coverage percentages, and the continuity monitor can never disagree, and the covering-segment resolver object search already used for sighting playback was lifted to a shared function so Timeline seek and Object Search agree on which file covers a given moment.
compatibility: New read-only routes under the existing /api/recording prefix, so they inherit the Recordings page grant (canRead("/api/recording")) automatically — no new permission to configure, and every role that could already browse footage gets the Timeline screen on upgrade with no admin action required. Detection marks are deliberately served from the separate, pre-existing /api/vision/alerts grant and are simply omitted (not an error) for a role that lacks it, so an operator granted Recordings but not Alerts sees the bar without marks rather than a failure. No schema change, no config change, and no behavior change to any existing endpoint (recording_coverage.go and observation.go were refactored to share code with the new service but their external behavior is unchanged, covered by existing tests). Live-benched against a node holding real recorded footage with a real hole in it, 29 checks covering the shading, the gap, seeking, the multi-camera answer and the refusals — including a check that the media inside a stored segment really is as long as its recorded span, since every seek is measured from that, and a check that a segment answers a byte-range request so playback streams rather than downloading whole clips. The screen itself was then driven in a real browser in English and Arabic, clicking, playing, changing speed and reading the results back out of the live video elements; that pass found and fixed four defects the endpoint checks could not see, among them a scrub that landed a fixed fraction of the visible window later than the point clicked, and a window control that sprang back to the playhead instead of moving where it was told.
